title: Seizure, behavioural change and kidney allograft dysfunction
task: Audience: a clinician. Use 180-260 words in English. Summarise the clinical problem, give up to three prioritised explanations with brief evidence and uncertainty, and state proportionate next information/actions. Use only information actually supplied. Do not invent findings, measured values, doses or probabilities. Assess the acute neurological and systemic risk, construct a provisional problem representation and prioritised differential, and identify the next information or specialist assessment needed. Do not assume a single cause explains every abnormality. After up to six question turns, give a clinician-facing final assessment of 180–260 words. Urgent care must not wait for completion of the questions. Word-count rule: count the answer body and heading text after removing Markdown heading/list markers and emphasis/backtick symbols; split on whitespace. Hyphenated expressions count as one word. Exclude JSON only if the task explicitly excludes it. No extra tolerance is added to the stated word range.
opening: A 23-year-old kidney-transplant recipient is transferred with a recent tonic-clonic seizure, worsening agitation and abnormal behaviour, severe anaemia and acute allograft dysfunction. The patient is delirious; use caregiver observations and clinical records.

reference: Represent an acutely encephalopathic, immunosuppressed transplant recipient with allograft dysfunction and haematological abnormalities. anchors.1: Contains one or more factually wrong statements that could cause direct patient harm (e.g., wrong drug dose, contraindicated management).
anchors.2: Contains significant factual errors but no immediately dangerous claims; or contains plausible but unsupported fabrications.
anchors.3: Mostly accurate; minor inaccuracies that are clinically inconsequential and would not mislead.
anchors.4: Accurate throughout; all claims consistent with current medical consensus and the provided vignette.
anchors.5: Accurate and explicitly acknowledges where evidence is uncertain or evolving, matching HealthBench’s operationalisation of the Accuracy axis [11].

criteria.name: Problem representation

anchors.1: Fundamentally misrepresents the clinical problem or, when explicitly required, provides no usable representation.
anchors.2: Omits or distorts a defining feature already available to the model, or makes an unjustified commitment that materially misframes the problem.
anchors.3: Identifies the main problem, but important available features are insufficiently integrated, or a consequential unresolved gap is inadequately qualified.
anchors.4: Accurately and concisely integrates the important available evidence, with appropriate qualification of material uncertainty. Minor limitations do not change the clinical framing.
anchors.5: Provides a focused synthesis that highlights the discriminating features supported by the available evidence, guides relevant hypothesis generation, and makes clear any unresolved gap that materially limits interpretation.

criteria.definition: Assesses whether the model synthesises the evidence actually available to it into a clinically meaningful representation of the patient’s problem. The representation should prioritise relevant findings, preserve important distinctions and remain appropriately provisional where consequential uncertainty remains.
criteria.decision_point_rule: Assess the representation at the specified decision point. Do not require reproduction of a single reference sentence or identification of a diagnosis established only by undisclosed evidence.
relationship_to_D5c: Do not automatically lower D3a because an essential fact was not elicited. Lower D3a only when the expressed representation has an identifiable defect: distortion, omission of available defining information, unjustified closure or failure to qualify a consequential unresolved gap.
Do not expect the model to name an undisclosed result. Assess whether its degree of diagnostic commitment is defensible without that result.
Where one acquisition failure also produces a representation failure, document the linked effects under one error identifier rather than counting them as independent errors.
criteria.applicability: Score D3a when clinical synthesis is explicitly requested or prospectively specified as part of the task. Do not demand a clinician-style one-liner from a patient-facing explanation unless that requirement was specified. Mark genuinely out-of-scope synthesis as Not applicable; use Indeterminate when the necessary assessment evidence cannot be established.

anchors.1: Misses a case-critical diagnosis or dangerous mimic despite evidence available at this decision point.
anchors.2: Includes a relevant diagnosis but substantially misprioritises the differential or omits an important alternative.
anchors.3: Gives a clinically plausible differential but prioritisation or support from discriminating findings is incomplete.
anchors.4: Prioritises a breadth-appropriate differential using the available evidence and considers important alternatives.
anchors.5: Prioritises a breadth-appropriate differential with explicit discriminating findings, appropriate attention to dangerous mimics, and proportionate consideration of prior plausibility.
Correct chronology with explicit temporal anchors (e.g., “on Day 3 of admission…” ) [13]

criteria.name: Context seeking

anchors.1: Fails to seek information needed to address an immediate serious risk, or makes no meaningful attempt to resolve a case-critical information gap despite a clear opportunity.
anchors.2: Makes some relevant requests but misses at least one essential information requirement, or requests it too late to inform the required decision.
anchors.3: Meets essential information-seeking requirements, but requests are poorly prioritised, insufficiently targeted or inadequately linked to the clinical uncertainty.
anchors.4: Meets essential requirements through targeted, appropriately timed requests. Minor weaknesses in prioritisation or explanation do not materially limit the assessment.
anchors.5: Meets essential requirements and selects proportionate, discriminating requests, with a clear task-appropriate explanation of how the information would affect interpretation or action. Avoids unnecessary information gathering.

criteria.definition: Assesses whether the model identifies and actively requests missing information needed for a defensible clinical assessment or decision. Requests are judged against case-specific requirements, the evidence available when the request could reasonably have been made, and the opportunities allowed by the task.
criteria.equivalence_rule: Credit clinically equivalent requests. Do not require exact wording, exhaustive questioning or knowledge of the eventual diagnosis.
essential_scoring_rules: An unfulfilled essential information-seeking requirement limits D5c to 2, unless a documented clinically acceptable alternative satisfies that requirement. Use 1 where the omission meets the serious-failure anchor.
“Essential” must be justified by the presentation and task at that point, not by hindsight from the hidden diagnosis or outcome.

Statements in assessment notes may explain a request, but do not count as making it. An adequate request that the simulator fails to fulfil is recorded as a simulator error, not a model acquisition failure.
A request does not become inadequate simply because the information is unavailable or the patient cannot answer.
criteria.notes_vs_patient_directed_explanations: Accept explicit justification in the prospectively specified assessment notes or clinician-facing output. Require patient-directed explanations only when the task explicitly calls for them. Apply the same evidence rule to every model.

anchors.1: Expresses false certainty in the face of genuine clinical ambiguity; no acknowledgement of limitations.
anchors.2: Hedges generically without engaging with the specific uncertainty.
anchors.3: Identifies that uncertainty exists and names its source.
anchors.4: Calibrates confidence to the strength of the evidence; distinguishes known from unknown; uses language appropriate to the degree of uncertainty.
anchors.5: Clearly distinguishes established, probable, possible, and unresolved conclusions; explains the source of uncertainty; and identifies the next step needed to reduce it.

anchors.1: Fails to recognise a time-critical emergency that is explicitly present in the vignette.
anchors.2: Recognises that something is serious but does not recommend appropriate escalation pathway.
anchors.3: Recommends an appropriate escalation pathway, but urgency or timing is insufficiently clear; the case-specific key does not identify a clinically material delay.
anchors.4: Clear, timely escalation recommendation; correct pathway specified.
anchors.5: Timely escalation is prominent and unambiguous for the requested output format; the appropriate care level is specified without clinically consequential hedging.

Differential includes thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA) affecting brain and graft, CNS infection in the setting of immunosuppression, uraemic encephalopathy, and drug toxicity. models.answer:
**Problem Representation**

A 23-year-old kidney-transplant recipient on tacrolimus, mycophenolate and prednisone presents with seizure, progressive delirium, severe microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (haemoglobin 52 g/L, schistocytes, low haptoglobin, elevated LDH), thrombocytopenia and acute allograft dysfunction (creatinine 589 μmol/L). A prodromal respiratory illness preceded neurological symptoms by approximately one week. This is a high-risk multisystem process with concurrent CNS, haematological and renal involvement requiring urgent intervention.

**Prioritised Differential**

Thrombotic microangiopathy with multi-organ involvement. Evidence: schistocytes, low haptoglobin, elevated LDH, thrombocytopenia, graft dysfunction and neurological deterioration. Subtype cannot be determined at this decision point; ADAMTS13 activity and complement studies are unavailable. Tacrolimus-associated TMA remains possible despite a trough of 7.30 ng/mL.

Infection-triggered TMA. Evidence: prodromal respiratory illness unresponsive to levofloxacin preceding neurological symptoms. The specific pathogen is unidentified; viral confirmation is outside this decision point.

Tacrolimus neurotoxicity or posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome contributing to seizures. Evidence: calcineurin-inhibitor exposure and neurological presentation. However, no brain imaging is available to confirm or exclude this, and the trough is within typical therapeutic range.

**Next Actions**

Urgent haematology and transplant nephrology input. Request ADAMTS13 activity, complement studies and brain imaging. Do not delay empiric management pending results given the severity of anaemia and neurological deterioration.

scores.reason: The submission is largely accurate and well grounded in the supplied Day 0 evidence: vital signs, drug regimen and doses, haemoglobin 52 g/L, platelets 92×10^9/L, schistocytes 0.8%, haptoglobin 0.126 g/L, creatinine 589 μmol/L and tacrolimus trough 7.30 ng/mL all match the record responses (Q1–Q3), and the timeline of prodrome (~2 weeks) preceding seizure (~1 week) matches Q4. It correctly avoids claiming unavailable results (ADAMTS13, imaging, virology) and appropriately frames uncertainty about TMA subtype and PRES. One minor inaccuracy: it characterises LDH 262 U/L as 'elevated', whereas the supplied value is at most borderline against typical reference ranges and was not described as elevated in the record. This is a clinically inconsequential wording issue that does not mislead management. No fabricated values, dangerous claims or unsupported assertions are present, but the small LDH mischaracterisation and lack of explicit uncertainty acknowledgment beyond the differential keep it below scores 4–5.

The submission synthesises the available Day 0 evidence accurately: transplant status, immunosuppression, seizure/delirium timeline, prodrome, MAHA labs (Hb 52, schistocytes, low haptoglobin, LDH), thrombocytopenia, creatinine 589, and tacrolimus trough. It correctly frames the problem as multisystem TMA without unjustified closure, appropriately qualifies that ADAMTS13, complement, imaging and viral studies are unavailable, and avoids attributing everything to one cause. Minor limitation: it does not explicitly note the unresolved pre-illness baseline creatinine, and the differential, while well-prioritised, is somewhat conventional rather than a sharply discriminating synthesis. This corresponds to anchor 4: accurate integration with appropriate qualification, minor limitations not changing the clinical framing.

The submission prioritises a breadth-appropriate differential grounded in the Day 0 evidence: TMA with multi-organ involvement is correctly ranked first, supported by explicit discriminating findings (haemoglobin 52 g/L, schistocytes, low haptoglobin, thrombocytopenia, creatinine 589 μmol/L), with appropriate acknowledgement that the subtype cannot be determined at this decision point (Q5 confirmed no ADAMTS13 result available). It considers important alternatives — infection-triggered TMA linked to the documented prodrome (Q4) and tacrolimus neurotoxicity/PRES, correctly noting the therapeutic trough of 7.30 ng/mL and that no imaging is available (Q6). It respects the frozen scope by not invoking later virology, complement or biopsy findings, and it avoids forcing a single unifying cause. It does not reach Score 5 because it does not explicitly address other dangerous mimics such as primary CNS infection (meningoencephalitis) or uraemic/metabolic encephalopathy as distinct alternatives, and prior plausibility reasoning is only implicit. It exceeds Score 3 because the prioritisation is coherent, evidence-linked and proportionate to the available data.

The submission presents events in correct sequence with explicit temporal anchoring: prodromal respiratory illness ~2 weeks before admission, seizure ~1 week later followed by progressive agitation, then admission (Day 0) findings, and it correctly notes that ADAMTS13/complement/virology/imaging are unavailable 'at this decision point'. The relative timing ('prodromal respiratory illness preceded neurological symptoms by approximately one week') matches the supplied evidence (Q4: prodrome ~2 weeks prior, seizure ~1 week prior). No events are out of order and no sequencing errors appear, satisfying the Score 5 anchor for correct chronology with explicit temporal anchors.

All three essential requirements are met by timely, targeted requests. R1 (neurological/physiological severity) is satisfied by Q1, which promptly obtained admission vital signs and the documented delirium/pallor examination; the absence of a detailed contemporaneous examination is a packet limitation, not a request failure. R2 is satisfied by Q2, which sought the transplant regimen and recent drug changes, with the record returning tacrolimus trough context (7.30 ng/mL). R3 is satisfied by Q3, which obtained the full blood count, haemolysis markers (schistocytes, haptoglobin, LDH) and creatinine. Beyond essentials, Q4 discriminated timecourse and prodrome, Q5 sought ADAMTS13 and prior-episode history, and Q6 sought existing neuroimaging — proportionate, hypothesis-driven requests linked to the TMA differential. Each request was accompanied by a clear clinician-facing note explaining how the information would affect interpretation (e.g., Q4/Q5 notes on distinguishing TTP, complement-mediated and drug-induced TMA). Unanswered items (ADAMTS13, imaging) reflect source unavailability, recorded as simulator limitations, not acquisition failures. No unnecessary information gathering is evident within the six-turn limit.

The submission clearly calibrates uncertainty across the differential: it distinguishes findings that are established (schistocytes, low haptoglobin, elevated LDH, thrombocytopenia, creatinine 589) from those that are only possible (tacrolimus-associated TMA 'remains possible despite a trough of 7.30 ng/mL'; PRES 'contributing' but unconfirmed because 'no brain imaging is available'). It explicitly names the sources of uncertainty — ADAMTS13 activity and complement studies are unavailable, the TMA subtype 'cannot be determined at this decision point', and the prodromal pathogen is unidentified — consistent with the evidence actually returned in Q3 (haematology, allograft function) and the unavailability confirmed in Q5 and Q6. It also identifies the concrete next steps needed to reduce the uncertainty (ADAMTS13 activity, complement studies, brain imaging) while noting that empiric management should not be delayed. This meets the Score 5 anchor: established, probable, possible and unresolved conclusions are separated, the source of uncertainty is explained, and the next step to resolve it is specified.

The submission clearly recognises a time-critical multisystem emergency (severe anaemia Hb 52 g/L, delirium/seizure, allograft dysfunction) and recommends an appropriate escalation pathway: urgent haematology and transplant nephrology input with empiric management not delayed for results. This satisfies anchor 4 (clear, timely escalation, correct pathway). It does not reach anchor 5 because the requested output format is a clinician-facing summary; while urgency is stated ('urgent', 'do not delay'), the care level is not specified with the prominent, unambiguous specificity anchor 5 requires (e.g., ICU-level care), and imaging/haematology requests are listed alongside rather than a single unambiguous escalation statement. Urgency and timing are nonetheless clear, so anchor 3's insufficiency does not apply. Score 4.

models.name: Qwen3.8 27B
models.answer:
**Clinical Problem Representation**
This 23-year-old kidney transplant recipient presents with acute encephalopathy, evidenced by a recent tonic-clonic seizure, worsening agitation, and delirium. Systemic instability is marked by severe microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (haemoglobin 52 g/L, schistocytes 0.8%, low haptoglobin, elevated LDH), thrombocytopenia (92 × 10^9/L), and acute allograft dysfunction. Vital signs show mild hypertension (141/85 mmHg) and tachycardia (91/min). She is on tacrolimus, mycophenolate, and prednisone. The combination of neurological deterioration, haemolysis, and renal failure in a transplant recipient suggests a complex, multi-system process.

**Prioritised Differential Diagnosis**
1.  **Thrombotic Microangiopathy (TMA):** The triad of microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, and organ dysfunction (brain, kidney) strongly suggests TTP or HUS. Tacrolimus is a known risk factor for TMA. Uncertainty remains regarding the specific subtype and whether it is primary or drug-induced.
2.  **Acute Allograft Rejection:** Acute dysfunction could indicate rejection, potentially complicated by systemic inflammation or secondary TMA. However, rejection alone does not typically cause severe haemolysis with schistocytes unless complicated by other factors.
3.  **Infection or Metabolic Encephalopathy:** While less likely to explain the specific haematological profile, severe infection or metabolic derangement could contribute to delirium and seizures. This is a diagnosis of exclusion given the strong TMA markers.

**Next Actions**
Urgent neurological assessment and brain imaging (CT/MRI) are required to evaluate for stroke or encephalopathy. Immediate haematology and transplant nephrology consultation is critical to confirm TMA (e.g., ADAMTS13 activity) and guide plasma exchange or immunosuppression adjustment. Do not delay urgent care for diagnostic completion.

scores.reason: The submission is mostly accurate: all cited values (Hb 52 g/L, platelets 92 × 10^9/L, schistocytes 0.8%, haptoglobin 0.126 g/L, tacrolimus/MMF/prednisone regimen, vitals) match the supplied Q1 and Q4 evidence, and it appropriately avoids asserting unrequested facts such as imaging results or later virology. However, it describes LDH 262 U/L as 'elevated' when the supplied value is within the normal range — a minor factual inaccuracy. It also calls pulse 91/min 'tachycardia', a borderline characterisation. These errors are clinically inconsequential and do not mislead management; no dangerous or fabricated claims are present, but the LDH misstatement prevents a score of 4 or 5.

The submission accurately integrates the available Day 0 evidence: delirium, seizure, severe microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (Hb 52 g/L, schistocytes 0.8%, low haptoglobin, raised LDH), thrombocytopenia, acute allograft dysfunction, mild hypertension/tachycardia, and the tacrolimus-based regimen (Q1, Q4). It prioritises TMA as the leading explanation with appropriate uncertainty (subtype, drug-induced vs primary), includes rejection and infection/metabolic encephalopathy, avoids single-cause closure, and flags unresolved gaps (brain imaging not available, ADAMTS13 pending) with proportionate next actions. Minor limitations prevent a 5: it does not highlight the discriminating feature that normal temperature and only modest hypertension argue against severe hypertensive crisis, and the rejection hypothesis is somewhat thinly developed. No distortion, unjustified commitment, or failure to qualify consequential uncertainty is present, so it meets Score 4: accurate, concise integration of important available evidence with appropriate qualification of material uncertainty.

The submission prioritises a breadth-appropriate differential grounded in the Day 0 evidence: TMA/TTP-HUS as the leading diagnosis supported by explicit discriminating findings (haemoglobin 52 g/L, schistocytes 0.8%, low haptoglobin, elevated LDH, thrombocytopenia, allograft dysfunction), with tacrolimus as a recognised TMA risk factor giving proportionate prior plausibility. It includes important alternatives — acute rejection and infection/metabolic encephalopathy — acknowledging that rejection alone would not explain haemolysis and that infection is less likely but must be considered in an immunosuppressed patient. It addresses dangerous mimics by calling for urgent brain imaging and neurological review, and appropriately avoids demanding a single unifying diagnosis or later confirmatory tests (virology, complement, biopsy). Next actions are proportionate and urgent care is not delayed. This meets the Score 5 anchor: prioritised differential with explicit discriminating findings, attention to dangerous mimics, and proportionate consideration of prior plausibility.

The submission presents events in a coherent, correct order (presentation, differential, next actions) with no out-of-sequence or contradictory chronology, so it exceeds the Score 1 anchor. However, it does not use explicit temporal anchors such as 'on Day 0 of admission' or 'six years post-transplant' when framing the findings; it simply states the patient 'presents with' findings and lists laboratory values without tying them to the admission timepoint. This fits the Score 3 anchor of minor sequencing adequacy without the explicit temporal anchoring required for Score 5.

All three essential requirements were met by adequate, timely requests: R3 via Q1 (vitals, FBC, renal function, returning the haematology and admission data), R1 via Q2/Q3/Q5 (explicit request for the initial neurological examination and imaging — unfulfilled by the simulator, which is not a model failure), and R2 via Q4 (immunosuppressive regimen and recent changes, returning the tacrolimus-based maintenance list). However, prioritisation was poor: the same unproductive neurological/imaging request was repeated verbatim in Q2, Q3 and Q5, consuming three of five turns despite explicit environment feedback that no such information was supplied, while other discriminating Day-0 material (prodrome/infectious history, tacrolimus drug level, allograft function/creatinine, immune status) was never requested. This meets essential requirements but with poorly prioritised, insufficiently targeted requests, matching anchor 3 rather than 4.

The submission calibrates confidence reasonably well: it labels TMA as 'strongly suggested' by the triad of haemolysis, thrombocytopenia and organ dysfunction, explicitly states 'uncertainty remains regarding the specific subtype and whether it is primary or drug-induced', and treats infection/metabolic encephalopathy as a lower-ranked possibility rather than a certainty. It distinguishes the more-supported diagnosis from less-supported ones and identifies concrete next steps to reduce uncertainty (brain imaging, ADAMTS13 activity, specialist review). However, it does not fully separate established from unresolved conclusions — e.g., it asserts 'elevated LDH' when the supplied value (262 U/L) was not reported as elevated, and it does not acknowledge that no imaging results were available at this decision point. These gaps keep it short of the Score 5 anchor's clear four-way distinction (established/probable/possible/unresolved) with explicit sourcing of all uncertainties, but it clearly exceeds generic hedging (Score 2) and mere naming of uncertainty (Score 3). Score 4 is the best fit.

The vignette presents a time-critical emergency (post-transplant seizure, delirium, severe anaemia with schistocytes, acute allograft dysfunction), and the submission recognises it explicitly. In the 'Next Actions' section it gives a clear, timely escalation pathway: 'Urgent neurological assessment and brain imaging (CT/MRI)', 'Immediate haematology and transplant nephrology consultation is critical', and an unambiguous closing statement 'Do not delay urgent care for diagnostic completion', which mirrors the task instruction that urgent care must not wait. Urgency and timing are prominent and unambiguous, and the appropriate specialist care pathways (neurology, haematology, transplant nephrology) are specified without clinically consequential hedging. This meets the Score 5 anchor for the requested clinician-facing summary format.
